subject: Accounting
title: Mark-to-Market Manipulation
description: A fast breakdown of Mark-to-Market Manipulation for builders.

hook.text: Enron booked the entire future profit of a 20-year contract on the day it was signed.

buildup.text: Mark-to-market accounting records assets at current market value—updated constantly.

discovery.text: Enron applied this to long-term energy contracts, estimating future profits and booking them today.

twist.text: Those estimates were wildly optimistic. When reality arrived, the profits evaporated.

climax.text: Mark-to-market isn't inherently wrong, but Enron abused it beyond all reasonable limits.

punchline.text: Counting chickens before they hatch is dangerous accounting.

quiz.question: How did Enron abuse mark-to-market accounting?
options: It booked future estimated profits immediately

details.summary: Mark-to-market accounting values assets at current market prices rather than historical cost. This topic explains how Enron and others exploited this legitimate method to book future profits immediately by using aggressive—and sometimes fictitious—valuations.
details.whyItMatters: Mark-to-market is a valid accounting method, but when applied to illiquid or long-term contracts, it creates enormous room for manipulation. The technique was central to Enron's fraud.
takeaways: Enron used mark-to-market to book the entire expected profit of 20-year contracts on day one
Valuing illiquid assets at 'market' is problematic when no active market exists to verify prices
After Enron, regulators tightened rules around fair value measurement and disclosure

faq.question: What is mark-to-market accounting?
faq.answer: Mark-to-market accounting values assets and liabilities at their current market price rather than original purchase price. While appropriate for liquid securities with observable market prices, it becomes problematic for unique or illiquid assets where values are estimated.

faq.question: How did Enron abuse mark-to-market accounting?
faq.answer: Enron applied mark-to-market to long-term energy contracts, booking decades of projected future profits on the day a deal was signed. Since these contracts had no active market, Enron used its own internal models to set valuations—essentially choosing its own profit numbers.
